body_markdown: *The Fast and the Furious* changed everything for me. I was always into cars, but I remember coming out of the theater after seeing the first movie and wanting to get my car sideways and just be part of that world. It wasn’t only the cars—it was the feeling. It reminds you of being younger, having fun, hanging out with friends, and doing dumb stuff with cars. I’ve been collecting cars since I was a kid. At 15, I already had three cars. I had been a hardcore muscle car guy. I loved Chargers, GTOs, Camaros, Chevelles—all that stuff, American muscle. I always appreciated imports, but they weren’t really my thing until I started collecting them. Then I realized how fast the imports actually are. *Welcome to the[Hagerty Movies and Cars Celebration](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/welcome-to-the-hagerty-movies-and-cars-celebration/) , where we highlight and explore the relationship between[cars and the silver screen](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/movies-and-cars/) .* All that said, I ended up going down the rabbit hole of collecting *Fast & Furious* replicas by chance. I was contacted by a guy who had inherited a collection of such cars from his business partner who passed away. He didn’t want them, so I ended up buying 15 cars all at once. The first one I loaded up was the gray Skyline GT-R from the beginning of *2 Fast 2 Furious* . I absolutely love that car. From there, things kind of snowballed. Alex McInnes/The Car Creative Alex McInnes/The Car Creative Alex McInnes/The Car Creative People found out that I had these cars, and suddenly I was getting calls and emails offering me more. Now I have several vehicles actually used on-screen, including Don Omar and Tego Calderón’s six-wheel heist truck, the Chevelle wheelie car driven by Vin Diesel, and the BMW 5 Series from the fourth film. I also have the *Fast Five* Charger, and another Charger that was used as a green-screen crash car. For me, the iconic cars are mostly from the first five movies. After that, the franchise became more superhero than street racing. I wanted the cars people really remembered. The screen-used cars are a bit of a mixed bag as far as condition goes, but they are nonetheless the crown jewels of my collection. The BMW hero car, for example, looks great—the interior is nice and the body is solid. But it’s a 528i six-cylinder dressed up to look like an M5. The stunt cars are usually the opposite. They’ll have rough interiors, but bigger engines needed for burnouts and action scenes. Above: Cameron leans against the Nissan Skyline GT-R from *2 Fast 2 Furious* , which he identifies as his favorite, if he were forced to pick just one. Alex McInnes/The Car Creative The Chevelle wheelie car was a surprise. I imagined it being this incredible machine, but when I got it, it had a 350-cubic-inch V-8 making maybe 250 horsepower. The wheelie effect came from weights welded to the back of the frame. That’s how they do it. They throw the weights on there, and literally all you had to do was touch the gas. I couldn’t leave it like that. We tore it apart, installed a 620-hp 572-cubic-inch V-8, added a six-speed transmission, upgraded the suspension, and restored everything. It still looks exactly like it did in the movie, but now it’s a genuinely badass car. That’s my philosophy. I want to drive these things. I want to take it to a show or do burnouts with it. And that’s what people want to see too. They don’t want to see a car rolled off the trailer and surrounded by stanchions. Alex McInnes/The Car Creative If you look at my Instagram, you’ll see the Chargers doing burnouts. I don’t treat these cars like museum pieces. I take them out, break them, fix them, and enjoy them. We recently finished a replica of the Supra from the first movie. I took it out, did burnouts and donuts, and blew up the clutch. Now I have to fix it. For my replicas, all the cars use proper components: original-style wheels, correct wings, seats, body kits—everything. It’s a ton of work. Take Sun Kang’s Mazda RX-7 from *The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift* . Finding the correct wheels took me two years. You’ll occasionally find a set, but people want 20 grand for 30-year-old wheels. The silver-and-purple Skyline from *Tokyo Drift* was the same story: six months to find the right wheels. I paid around $3500 for a beat-up set, restored them, added tires, and suddenly I was $8500 into the wheels. But it makes all the difference. People notice. Cameron dived headfirst into his *Fast & Furious* obsession by purchasing a collection of 15 cars. From there, “things just snowballed,” he recalls. Alex McInnes/The Car Creative Every time I get into a car from my collection, I think, “This is my favorite.” But if I had to choose one, I’d pick the gray *2 Fast 2 Furious* Skyline GT-R. There’s just something about it. It wasn’t even in the movie for that long, but it’s so connected to Paul Walker. People absolutely love that car. The Charger is right up there too. It’s just iconic. For a long time, people said *Tokyo Drift* was one of the weaker movies in the franchise (not me—I always liked it). Now those cars are some of the most popular ones I own. People go crazy when they see Kang’s RX-7, the Hulk van, the drift Evo. That movie really came into its own over the past 10 years. If I could get one car, it’d be the original, screen-used Charger from the first movie. The car that started it all. I’ve had opportunities to buy Chargers from later movies, and I passed on a few that I probably shouldn’t have. But if I could get the actual first-movie Charger, that would be incredible. And if I can’t get it?
